power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Purpose: To compare multimodal large language models (MLLMs), vision foundation models (VFMs), and contrastive vision-language models (VLMs) for ophthalmic image interpretation with no labeled examples (zero-shot) or as few as 10 labeled examples per class (10-shot).
Subjects: 4 public datasets (UCSD, IDRiD, REFUGE, ASOCT-MSDC) and 3 private datasets (OHTS, BPEI-DLS, WashU-OCT) of anterior-and posterior-segment ophthalmic imaging.
Methods: Nine AI models were evaluated across 3 architectural families: MLLMs (Qwen3.8-27B, GLM-5.3-Flash, Gemma-4-31B-it), VFMs (DINOv3, RETFound, VisionFM), and VLMs (CLIP, EyeCLIP, SigLIP2).
Models were assessed on disease classification, disease risk and severity grading, anatomical assessment, and lesion localization in fundus and OCT imaging.
MLLMs were also compared with a 3D VFM (OCTCube-M) for whole-volume OCT classification.
MLLMs were evaluated zero-shot and 10-shot, without additional training.
Vision models (VFMs and VLMs) were adapted by linear probing and fine-tuning on the same 10-shot set and on the full training dataset (FD).
Disease classification performance (macro-averaged F1, AUROC, quadratic weighted kappa [QWK]), anatomical localization accuracy, and cross-dataset generalization.
Results: For retinal OCT disease classification, 10-shot MLLMs achieved a macro-F1 of 0.94, versus 0.59 (10-shot) and 0.96 (FD) for vision models.
For diabetic retinopathy and macular edema grading, 10-shot MLLMs achieved QWKs of 0.69 and 0.73, versus 0.48 and 0.57 (10shot) and 0.72 and 0.79 (FD) for vision models.
For lesion localization, 10-shot MLLMs achieved an F1 of 0.75, versus 0.70 (10-shot) and 0.86 (FD) for vision models.
For vertical cup-to-disc ratio estimation (OHTS), zero-shot MLLMs achieved a mean absolute error of 0.14, versus 0.21 (10-shot) for vision models.
For whole-volume OCT classification (WashU-OCT), zero-shot MLLMs achieved a macro-F1 of 0.71, versus 0.50 (10-shot) and 0.82 (FD) for vision models.

Deep learning has enabled accurate detection of several eye diseases from color fundus photographs (CFPs) and optical coherence tomography (OCT), including diabetic retinopathy (DR), age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and glaucomatous optic neuropathy. [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] However, developing and adapting these systems have traditionally required large amounts of labeled data. 6, 7 Several prominent systems, for example, were developed using tens of thousands to more than 100,000 expert-graded fundus photographs 1, 2 or thousands of labeled OCT volumes. 6 Expert annotation is time-consuming, 7 grader disagreement makes reference standards imperfect, 8 and public ophthalmic datasets are geographically concentrated, with incomplete reporting of patient demographics and labeling methods. 9 In addition, performance can vary substantially across algorithms and screening sites, which supports local validation before deployment. 10 Vision foundation models (VFMs), such as RETFound and VisionFM, may reduce the need for new task-specific annotations by learning from large image collections before being adapted to specific clinical tasks. [11] [12] [13] [14] RETFound, for example, was pretrained on 1.6 million unlabeled retinal images and, when adapted to ophthalmic tasks, outperformed comparison models while needing fewer labeled images. 13 Contrastive vision-language models (VLMs), such as CLIP, instead learn to match images with paired text, which allows them to classify an image by comparing it with written descriptions of each disease category. 15, 16 In ophthalmology, VLMs such as FLAIR and EyeCLIP have performed well when adapted with few labeled images, following pretraining on large ophthalmic imaging datasets. 17, 18 Generative multimodal large language models (MLLMs), a class of models distinct from VFMs and VLMs, 19 may reduce labeled data requirements even further.

text.text: By connecting a vision encoder to a large language model, an MLLM can follow written instructions about an image and respond in free text. 20, 21 MLLMs can learn a new task from a few labeled examples in the prompt without retraining, an approach known as in-context learning. 22, 23 General-purpose MLLMs such as GPT-4o and Gemini can interpret ophthalmic images, although performance has varied by disease, imaging type and task, [24] [25] [26] [27] and adding examples to the prompt has improved it in some evaluations but not in others. 28, 29 Additionally, many of these evaluations used proprietary models accessed through the developer's cloud service. 23, 24, 27, 28 Sending images containing protected health information to an external cloud service for processing on behalf of a covered institution requires a business associate agreement and other applicable safeguards under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). 30, 31 Developers may also change or discontinue access to proprietary models after validation. 32 Open-weight MLLMs, whose model weights are publicly released, can instead run entirely on an institution's own hardware. 21, 32 Such locally deployed models keep both patient data and the model under institutional control, which may ease privacy and regulatory concerns about their clinical use. 21, 32 Evidence remains limited on whether locally deployed MLLMs match VFMs and VLMs across diverse ophthalmic tasks and datasets.

text.text: We therefore sought to benchmark local, open-weight MLLMs against VLMs and VFMs across a wide variety of ophthalmic image analysis tasks on both public and private datasets.
This study was conducted in accordance with the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Washington University in St.
Louis.
Due to the retrospective nature of the study, which involved the analysis of previously collected clinical data, the IRB waived the requirement for informed consent.
All analyses were performed on a secured HIPAA-compliant local GPU server.

We conducted a benchmark study to evaluate the performance of emerging generative MLLMs relative to established vision models (VFMs and VLMs) for ophthalmic image interpretation tasks across 7 imaging datasets (4 public and 3 private).

Tasks included disease classification, disease risk and severity grading, anatomical measurements, and lesion localization in CFPs, posterior-segment OCT, and anterior-segment OCT (AS-OCT), as well as multi-image classification of real-world clinical OCT volumes.
A primary aim of this study was to assess how model performance changed with the number of labeled examples, such as images with known diagnoses, from which a model can learn a new task.
First, models were evaluated without any labeled examples from the task's dataset (zero-shot evaluation).
Second, models were evaluated after being given 10 labeled examples per class (10-shot evaluation).
To ensure a fair comparison, the examples provided to MLLMs were the same examples provided to vision models, for each task and random seed (42-46).
For a complete evaluation, vision models were also evaluated after being given all available labeled examples (full-data adaptation).
This was not performed for MLLMs, as current models cannot accept thousands of example images within a single prompt.
MLLMs and vision models learned new tasks from these labeled examples in different ways.
MLLMs received written task instructions and the labeled examples within a prompt, from which they generated predictions without any additional training, an approach known as in-context learning.

In contrast, vision models underwent additional training on the labeled examples in one of three ways, which differ in how much of the pretrained model is changed: linear probing, in which the model's internal weights are kept fixed and only a simple final classification layer is trained; partial fine-tuning, in which the weights of the last few layers are also adjusted; and full fine-tuning, in which all weights are adjusted.

From the institutional Spectralis archive at Washington University in St Louis (199,486 imaging series from 19,588 patients; 2013-2026), we constructed the Washington University Clinical OCT Cohort (WashU-OCT), an enriched, single-disease cohort of 2,031 patients, one OCT volume each, with EHR-derived reference labels: 752 AMD, 627 DME, 353 epiretinal membrane (ERM), and 299 healthy.
Labels were assigned from eye-specific historical ICD-10 diagnoses and refined by rule-based screening of clinical notes.
The dataset was partitioned at the patient level into a training set (n = 426), a validation set (n = 183), and a held-out test set (n = 1,422).
Five 10-shot sets were constructed by randomly sampling 10 patients per class from the training set, using a different random seed for each set (seeds 42-46).
Full details of cohort construction are provided in Appendix 3 (WashU OCT Cohort Construction).
Three MLLMs were evaluated in the zero-shot setting, with each OCT volume represented by 25 B-scans provided together in a single inference request.

OCTCube-M, a pretrained threedimensional OCT foundation model, served as the supervised comparator. 47 OCTCube-M was adapted by linear probing and partial fine-tuning using either a 10-shot set (10 labeled volumes per class) or the full training set, with checkpoints selected on the validation set.

text.text: All models were evaluated on the same held-out test set.
For disease classification tasks, macro-averaged F1 was the primary metric, supplemented by balanced accuracy and per-class metrics; for glaucoma discrimination, AUROC was the primary metric.
For grading classification tasks, quadratic-weighted kappa was the primary metric, supplemented by adjacent-grade accuracy.
For lesion localization, band-level F1 was the primary metric, supplemented by balanced accuracy.
For landmark localization, Euclidean distance error was the primary metric.
For anatomical measurement, vCDR mean absolute error (MAE) was the primary metric.
For few-shot evaluation, results were reported as the mean ± SD across random seeds, with bootstrap 95% CIs for key comparisons.
For MLLMs, unparseable responses were logged and reported separately as an invalid-response rate.
We evaluated ophthalmic image interpretation across three model families: VFMs, contrastive VLMs, and generative MLLMs.

Tasks included disease classification, disease risk and severity grading, anatomical measurements, anatomical landmark and lesion localization, cross-dataset generalization, and whole-volume OCT classification, across multiple imaging modalities.
Models were compared with no labeled examples (zero-shot), with the same 10 labeled examples per class (10-shot), and, for vision models, with all available labeled data (full-data adaptation).
Occlusion sensitivity analyses assessed which image regions influenced predictions.

Demonstrations did not consistently improve performance: GLM-5.3-Flash worsened from 0.104 to 0.163-0.169, whereas Gemma-4-31B-it improved from 0.150 to 0.122.

With full-data adaptation, DINOv3 achieved the lowest linear-probing MAE (0.074), while CLIP achieved the lowest overall MAE (0.050; 95% CI, 0.047-0.054) with full fine-tuning (Supplementary Appendix 1, C.1).
For glaucoma discrimination using predicted vCDR as a continuous screening score, zero-shot MLLMs achieved AUROCs of 0.810-0.828, highest for Qwen3.8-27B (0.828; 95% CI, 0.751-0.894).
With 10-shot in-context learning, AUROCs ranged from 0.785 to 0.816, compared with 0.830 (95% CI, 0.783-0.872) for VisionFM and 0.679 (95% CI, 0.630-0.721) for CLIP using linear probing.
Thus, zero-shot MLLMs approached the strongest 10-shot supervised probe without labeled examples.
With full-data partial fine-tuning, RETFound achieved the highest AUROC (0.970; 95% CI, 0.936-0.993).

VisionFM achieved the highest 10-shot probing AUROC despite higher vCDR MAE than RETFound (0.201 versus 0.140), indicating that measurement accuracy and discrimination were not directly aligned (Supplementary Appendix 1, C.2).

To assess demographic robustness, vCDR estimation error was examined across OHTS subgroups stratified by age, sex, and race (Supplementary Appendix 1, D.2).
MLLMs achieved lower MAE than 10-shot VisionFM across all subgroups.
Across models, MAE was lower among Black than White participants (GLM zero-shot, 0.127 vs.
0.148) and among male than female participants (0.133 vs.
0.147), whereas no clear age-related trend was observed.
Notably, the absolute Black-White MAE gap was 54.3% smaller for GLM zero-shot than for fully trained VisionFM (0.021 vs.
0.046), suggesting more consistent performance across racial subgroups.
These exploratory findings support the cross-dataset generalizability of MLLMs, although the underlying causes of demographic differences warrant further investigation.

GLM-5.3-Flash achieved accuracy of 0.730 (95% CI, 0.707-0.752) and macro-F1 of 0.710 (95% CI, 0.686-0.733), compared with 0.608 (95% CI, 0.584-0.634) and 0.496 (95% CI, 0.476-0.516), respectively, for Qwen3.8-27B, and 0.660 (95% CI, 0.635-0.684) and 0.631 (95% CI, 0.604-0.656), respectively, for Gemma-4-31B-it.
GLM-5.3-Flash achieved class-specific F1 scores of 0.854 for AMD, 0.709 for DME, 0.691 for ERM, and 0.586 for healthy retina.
Qwen3.8-27B performed substantially worse for ERM (F1, 0.039), frequently misclassifying ERM as healthy.
As a volumetric baseline, OCTCube-M, a three-dimensional Vision Transformer pretrained using masked autoencoding, processed volumes resized to 60 × 256 × 256 voxels.
With ten labeled volumes per class, linear probing achieved accuracy of 0.316 (95% CI, 0.304-0.328) and macro-F1 of 0.151 (95% CI, 0.145-0.156) across five random seeds.
Partial fine-tuning of the final two transformer blocks and classification head improved accuracy to 0.588 (95% CI, 0.573-0.602) and macro-F1 to 0.502 (95% CI, 0.489-0.513).

With full-data linear probing, OCTCube-M achieved an accuracy of 0.390 (95% CI, 0.364-0.416) and a macro-F1 of 0.230 (95% CI, 0.216-0.244), improving to 0.854 (95% CI, 0.835-0.872) and 0.822 (95% CI, 0.799-0.843), respectively, with partial fine-tuning (Figure 4D).

These findings demonstrate the potential for training-free MLLM classification of clinical OCT volumes while highlighting the benefits of supervised adaptation for dedicated volumetric models.

In this study, we built an evaluation harness to benchmark the performance of open-weight This study demonstrates several advances that build upon prior benchmark studies assessing MLLM performance on ophthalmic image interpretation.

Notably, the Foundation Ophthalmic Cross-Dataset Understanding under Shift (FOCUS) study previously characterized MLLMs on binary fundus classification across 10 public datasets, 19 while the RetinaGroundBench study characterized zero-shot visual grounding of OCT biomarkers by open-weight MLLMs. 48 Our present study expands on these foundations by evaluating MLLM performance using an incontext learning framework, in which models received clinical definitions and labeled examples matched across model families.

text.text: In addition, while prior studies have evaluated MLLM performance with CFPs and individual OCT B-scans, we expand the repertoire of assessed imaging modalities to include AS-OCT and whole OCT volumes.

Likewise, our study extends beyond previously studied tasks, such as binary classification and bounding-box grounding, to additional complex tasks, including severity grading, anatomical measurement, and disease status classification.

Whereas prior studies have shown a limited ability of MLLMs to perform bounding-box grounding of OCT biomarkers without low-rank adaptation (LoRA) fine tuning, 48 our work demonstrates that in-context learning allows MLLMs to perform region-level localization at a level similar to VFMs and VLMs trained on the same examples.

text.text: Altogether, our results mark a major progression in ophthalmic AI.

Task-specific deep learning models have required training on thousands of graded two-dimensional images or annotated OCT volumes to achieve expert-level performance for a limited number of ophthalmic tasks. [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] Moreover, despite a shift in much of this training burden to the pre-training phase for VFMs, our present study demonstrates that VFM performance still strongly depends on the amount of labeled training data provided for a given task. [11] [12] [13] [14] 17, 18 MLLMs offer a potential alternative to the heavy training requirements of other model architectures, since they can be directed to new tasks through prompting rather than training.

text.text: Several mechanisms may account for these results.
Large-scale multimodal pretraining aligns visual features with language, 15, 16 which may enable MLLMs to apply written disease definitions to images.

text.text: Prior work has linked zero-shot performance to the frequency of concepts in multimodal pretraining data. 49 This may help explain why common, well-described findings such as macular edema, drusen and optic disc cupping were recognized without examples, although we did not test this mechanism directly.

text.text: In-context examples may then align predictions with dataset-specific labeling conventions, allowing rapid adaptation to a new task without retraining or developing a specialized model.
Task format may also help explain why MLLMs localized lesions well but not the scleral spur.

Selecting among numbered regions, as in Set-of-Marks prompting, 46 may reduce the spatial demands placed on MLLMs relative to generating precise coordinates as text. 48 Together, these properties allow a single general-purpose MLLM to be applied to diverse ophthalmic tasks with only a few labeled examples.

text.text: Beyond label efficiency, zero-shot evaluation offers a different perspective on cross-dataset generalizability: rather than transferring a model adapted on one dataset to another, MLLMs can be evaluated directly on independent datasets without task-specific training.

Training-data contamination is a central concern in benchmarking MLLMs.

Evidence of contamination with widely used multimodal benchmarks has been reported in both open-weight and proprietary MLLMs. 50 Public ophthalmic datasets are additionally susceptible to leakage between training and test splits. 51 Public datasets remain essential for reproducibility and comparison across studies, and recent benchmarks, as well as our own, have relied on them. 19, 48 To address this issue, we utilized three non-publicly released datasets to evaluate model generalizability, which include the controlled access OHTS as well as the institutionally curated BPEI-DLS and WashU-OCT datasets.

text.text: On all three private datasets, MLLMs outperformed VFMs and VLMs at a matched label budget.
Furthermore, for OHTS, BPEI-DLS, and WashU-OCT, zero-shot MLLMs outperformed VFMs and VLMs trained on 10 labeled examples per class.
Therefore, the consistent performance between private and public datasets strengthens confidence that our public benchmark results reflect generalization rather than memorization.
Generalization also depends on whether performance holds across patient populations.
In this study, the 10 labeled examples per class were sampled randomly, without stratification by age, sex, race, or ethnicity, so a small example set could in principle limit generalizability.

However, zero-shot inference uses no examples, and as noted above, zero-shot MLLMs achieved the lowest vCDR error on OHTS, a multicamera US cohort in which 26% of participants were Black. 39 Moreover, 10-shot demonstrations drawn from REFUGE, a dataset of Chinese patients, 38 increased OHTS error only slightly relative to zero-shot inference (MAE, 0.150 vs 0.141).

text.text: Across race, sex, and age subgroups on OHTS, MLLMs achieved lower error than vision models adapted with the same 10 examples, and no subgroup's error exceeded the overall error by more than 0.02 (Supplementary Appendix 1, D.2).

Error was modestly lower among Black and male participants for all models, including the fully trained vision model, suggesting differences in image or optic disc characteristics between subgroups rather than model-specific bias.

Nevertheless, these analyses reflect performance on a single task, and because the demographic composition of MLLM pretraining data is undisclosed, selecting representative examples and validating models on target populations continues to remain important before clinical use.
This study has several limitations.
First, although the benchmark spanned multiple tasks, imaging modalities, and ocular diseases, it did not encompass all ophthalmic tasks.
Second, all tasks in this study involved findings that clinicians can recognize.
Fundus photographs also contain systemic information not readily quantified through routine clinical assessment.

In the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Study, standardized grading showed that retinal arteriolar narrowing was associated with current and past blood pressure, 52, 53 and deep learning has since been used to predict cardiovascular risk factors from fundus photographs. 54 Whether incontext learning can identify such signals was not tested here.

text.text: Third, we did not assess semantic segmentation.

MLLMs could represent segmentation masks as text, such as binary masks, but this approach has not been fully evaluated, so it remains uncertain whether dedicated segmentation models will remain better suited for this task.

Fourth, we adopted standardized evaluation protocols, using primarily linear probing with partial fine-tuning for selected arms, for few-shot VFM and VLM adaptation and in-context learning without parameter updates for MLLMs.

Although alternative fine-tuning strategies and prompt designs may influence performance, our objective was to compare model families under a matched label budget and consistent evaluation settings rather than optimize each model individually.
Finally, the field is evolving rapidly, and our results represent a single point in time.
With continued investment in general-purpose models, the advantage of MLLMs in label-limited settings may widen, although this will require reassessment as models and methods evolve.

text.text: Developing task-specific ophthalmic AI has often required substantial annotation effort, computational resources, machine learning expertise, and a dedicated model for each application, which can limit development to centers with those resources.

Because locally deployed MLLMs can be applied to new tasks using task-specific instructions and a small number of labeled examples, effort could shift from annotation and model training toward defining clinically meaningful questions, curating representative examples, and rigorously evaluating model outputs.

This shift could democratize ophthalmic AI, allowing clinicians to develop and validate tools for the questions most relevant to their own patients, including rare diseases with few labeled cases and underserved populations, while keeping patient data within the institution.

In conclusion, locally deployed, open-weight MLLMs with 10 labeled examples per class outperformed VFMs and VLMs trained on the same examples in most of the ophthalmic tasks evaluated and generalized to new datasets without retraining.
These findings highlight a broader opportunity: making advanced ophthalmic image analysis accessible without massive labeled 538 datasets or specialized model development.

If validated prospectively, these findings suggest 539 that the next phase of ophthalmic AI will be defined less by the size of labeled datasets and 540 more by how effectively general-purpose MLLMs are directed toward clinical needs.

The principal findings were first, that for OCT-based classification of retinal pathology as well as CFP-based severity and risk grading of DR and DME, MLLMs undergoing 10-shot in-context learning outperformed VFMs and VLMs trained on the same number of examples.
Furthermore, MLLMs with 10 examples also approached the performance of VFMs and VLMs adapted using substantially larger labeled datasets on selected classification and grading tasks.
